content.content:
1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side, runs around the chamber, and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential. In a further embodiment the device carries one or more stirring elements, and the vibration of the device acts through them to produce a constant forward motion of the device over the exposed face, so that the device advances from area to area without being pulled or guided at all. The device is held down by the pressure differential and, because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face, it remains free to move while it is held, which is what allows the vibration itself to carry it across the work.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential. In a further embodiment the device carries one or more stirring elements, and the vibration of the device acts through them to produce a constant forward motion of the device over the exposed face, so that the device advances from area to area without being pulled or guided at all. The device is held down by the pressure differential and, because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face, it remains free to move while it is held, which is what allows the vibration itself to carry it across the work.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

1	A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 3, through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken on line 4-4 of FIG. 3, at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and, where the vibration device 10 is moved by the operator, the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
54	
55	Handles
56	
57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.
58	
59	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.
64	
65	Embodiment with stirring elements
66	
67	FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The hold is not loosened to permit that motion: the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and the pressure differential continues to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the vibration device 10 advances, so the vibration coupling into the covering element 36 is not interrupted by the movement. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.
68	
69	In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.
70	
71	Method of use
72	
73	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44, or by the vibration acting through the stirring elements 48 to advance the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38.
74

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 3, through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken on line 4-4 of FIG. 3, at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and, where the vibration device 10 is moved by the operator, the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Embodiment with stirring elements

FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The hold is not loosened to permit that motion: the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and the pressure differential continues to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the vibration device 10 advances, so the vibration coupling into the covering element 36 is not interrupted by the movement. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44, or by the vibration acting through the stirring elements 48 to advance the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38.

13	Abstract: A device comprising a main body and vibration generating means mounted on the main body. 14	Claims: A device for moving along a wall surface, said device comprising a main body, means for providing a holding force for holding the device against the wall surface, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body, said vibration generating means being adapted to impart a lifting force in a direction away from a wall surface to reduce the holding force, said vibration generating means also imparting a force in a predetermined direction along the wall surface to the main body by the vibration it generates to move the main body in said predetermined direction along the wall surface, said vibration generating means being provided with a cylinder mechanism including a housing and a piston disposed movably within the housing, said cylinder mechanism being mounted on the main body of the device and being inclined at a predetermined angle to the wall surface, said lifting force extending in a direction away from the wall surface and said force in said predetermined direction along the wall surface being imparted by stretching and contraction of the cylinder mechanism. A device according to claim 1 including means for treating a wall surface. The device of claim 2 wherein said vibration generating means is provided with a cylinder mechanism including a housing and a piston disposed movably within the housing, said cylinder mechanism is mounted on the main body of the device while being inclined at a predetermined angle to the wall surface, and said force in a direction away from the wall surface and said force in said predetermined direction along the wall surface are imparted by the stretching and contraction of the cylinder mechanism. The device of claim 2 wherein the main body of the device is provided with a main body portion and a rotary securing portion mounted rotatably on the main body portion, said vibration generating means is secured to the rotary securing portion, and the moving direction of the main body of the device is switched over by rotating the rotary securing portion relative to the main body portion. The device of claim 5 wherein the rotary securing portion has provided therein an operating handle for rotating the rotary securing portion relative to the main body portion. The device of claim 5 wherein a driving source for rotating the main body portion and the rotary securing portion is provided in one of the main body portion and the rotary securing portion. content.text:
I've read the disclosure, the conversation, all ten draft sections plus `numerals.md`, all six figure briefs, the audit evidence, and every `prior_art/` file. Here is what I found.

**Source ledger (all traced):** every claim limitation traces to the disclosure — rigid base/first side/second side, motor on the first side, air-extraction mechanism on the first side in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, rigid low-friction loop/skirt at the perimeter (plastic, metal, PTFE, combinations), the non-sealing perimeter with continuous ingress, extraction that keeps the chamber sub-atmospheric under that ingress, the all-rigid transmission path free of rubber/foam, sliding while held, handles for guiding, the rope/wire/cable pulling element and decoupled control, and the stirring-element self-advance (conversation line 223). The four `[REF:...]` characterisations (DE-202021002652-U1, US-11408462-B2, US-10001245-B2, US-4934475-A, US-11247858-B2) each match text actually present in the corresponding `prior_art/` file. Numerals 10–48 are one-part-one-numeral across text, table and briefs, with ≤8 per sheet.

**What I could not verify:** `figures/` contains only the six Markdown briefs — there is no `rendered-*.png` anywhere in the workspace, so no pixel, leader or hatch inspection was possible. I reconciled the section-mark record for FIG. 3 against the brief instead: the marks are recorded in a 1000-unit native frame (vertical mark runs y=50→950), and rescaled into the 1400×900 raw frame the horizontal 2-2 line lands at raw y≈686 — inside the interior face between mid-height and the lower ring, extending past both outer edges (raw x≈70→1330 vs the ring's 141→1259), with arrows down; 4-4 lands at raw x≈980, between mid-width and the right ring, arrows left. Both match the brief, so I am **not** reporting the apparent "line stops inside the frame" or "line lies in the bottom band" defects that a raw-frame reading of those numbers would suggest.

input.summary: The text is in good shape: every independent and dependent claim limitation, every numbered part (10–48), and every described structure, material, relationship and embodiment traces to an exact passage in input/disclosure.md or to the inventor's stirring-element message in input/conversation.md; the stirring-element/autonomous-advance embodiment, the pulling element, the handles, the non-sealing rigid low-friction perimeter and the all-rigid transmission path are all affirmatively disclosed. All five cited references are characterised only in terms their own prior_art/ files contain. Terminology is consistent between claims, description, numeral table and briefs, and no figure is said to show something its brief does not contain. The defects are on the drawing side: no rendered sheet exists in the workspace for any of the six figures, and FIG. 6 — the stirring-element sheet relied on by the description and by claims 10 and 20 — has no entry at all in review/figure-audit-evidence.json, whose sheet-numbering ("n/6") and figure list otherwise cover only FIGS. 1–5. I therefore could not perform the required pixel, leader, hatch or section-mark inspection on any sheet; the FIG. 3 section-mark record, once rescaled from its native 1000-unit frame into the 1400×900 raw frame, does agree with the FIG. 3 brief, so I report no section-line defect.

But review/figure-audit-evidence.json contains records for only five figures — FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 — and there is no rendered-FIG-6.png in figures/ or anywhere else in the workspace. FIG. 6 is the only depiction of the stirring-element embodiment, which the description relies on ("The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6") and which claims 10 and 20 recite. Independent corroboration: the pre-run mechanical checks list FIG. 6 only under the leader-endpoint failures and omit it from the semantic-geometry list that names FIGS. 1–5, which is what one would expect if no FIG. 6 sheet was ever rendered or geometry-reviewed. The FIG. 6 brief itself is complete and internally consistent (numerals 10, 36, 48; schematic disclaimers confined to what the sources leave open), so no brief text needs to change.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. # Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

content.content:
1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	The first of two problems with existing tile vibration devices is that both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between that sliding base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	Vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting approach the holding of a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode, a control being provided that selectively switches the generator between the suction mode and the blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2]. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

content.content:
1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side, runs around the chamber, and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential. In a further embodiment the device carries one or more stirring elements, and the vibration of the device acts through them to produce a constant forward motion of the device over the exposed face, so that the device advances from area to area without being pulled or guided at all. The device is held down by the pressure differential and, because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face, it remains free to move while it is held, which is what allows the vibration itself to carry it across the work.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12
